desc:
A non-decreasing array (repeated values allowed) was cut at some position into a front part and a back part and the two parts were swapped, producing nums. For example [3, 4, 4, 5, 1, 1, 2, 3] comes from [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5].

Given nums and two integers lo ≤ hi, return how many elements v satisfy lo ≤ v ≤ hi (duplicates are counted every time). For the array above, lo = 2 and hi = 4 the answer is 5 (the values 2, 3, 3, 4, 4). Aim for O(log n) on typical inputs.
constraints: nums is a rotation of a non-decreasing array
hints: If you knew where the sorted order starts, the answer would be 'upper bound of hi' minus 'lower bound of lo' in the sorted view.
Find the start s (the single index whose left neighbour is larger, or 0). With ties, nums[mid] == nums[hi] means you cannot decide: if nums[hi - 1] > nums[hi] then s = hi, otherwise drop hi.
Count = (first virtual position with value > hi) - (first virtual position with value ≥ lo), reading virtual position j as nums[(s + j) % n].
editorial: Counting values in a range is the same in every rotation of the array, so rebuild the sorted view virtually: position j of the sorted order is nums[(s + j) % n], where s is the start of the sorted order.

Finding s with duplicates uses the 'compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]' search. A larger middle sends the window right; a smaller middle sends it left; a tie is resolved by checking whether hi is itself the start (nums[hi - 1] > nums[hi]) and otherwise discarding hi. This is O(log n) typically and O(n) in the worst case (for example an array of nearly all equal values).
Then two ordinary binary searches over virtual positions give a = number of values < lo and b = number of values ≤ hi. The answer is b - a. Space O(1).
